preamble: A table isn't something you draw in a document — it's a grid you declare. You don't sketch the lines; you tell Docs how many columns and rows you want and it lays the structure down for you. So the question isn't "where are the drawing tools" — it's "how do I add a new object to this page", which is a different question with a much simpler answer.
generalization: Anything that isn't typed text — a table, an image, a chart, a page break — gets added rather than formatted. Format changes what's already there; Insert brings something new into existence. Once you sort every control in a document editor into one of those two piles, you stop hunting through menus and start guessing correctly the first time.

steps.intent: Nothing on the page will become a table by being restyled — you're bringing a new object into the document that didn't exist a moment ago. Docs keeps all of those in one place: the menu for things you add rather than things you change.
hints: You're not altering any existing text. You're putting something new on the page — which menu is that whole job filed under?
The Insert menu, in the menu bar along the top, between View and Format.

wrongHints.Format: A reasonable guess, because a table looks like a formatting decision. But Format only acts on text that already exists — it can't create a grid that isn't there yet.
wrongHints.Edit: Edit holds actions performed on your document's content — undo, copy, paste, find. Adding a brand-new structure is a different kind of operation, and Docs files it separately.

steps.intent: Now pick the kind of object. Everything in this menu is something you can drop into the page, and the one you want has a small arrow beside it — because a table needs a size before it can exist, and that arrow leads to the grid where you choose it.
hints: You're looking for the item named after the thing itself, not for anything that summarises or charts your content.
Near the top of the Insert menu, just below Image.

wrongHints.Chart: A chart also arrives as a grid-shaped block and even carries data, which makes it a fair guess. But a chart is a picture of numbers — a table is a layout you type directly into.
wrongHints.Drawing: You could draw rectangles that look like a table, and people do. What you'd get is a picture — no cells, no typing, no rows you can add later.
